notes:
First version, in development: photographing the qualification scorecards printed by ianseo (the session, the distance and the cards per sheet asked first, in that order, the rest of the page showing once they are given), with the computer's camera or a phone, one or the whole sheet of a target at once (every grid of the photo is found and read in turn, a bar showing where each stands). The grids are found and straightened, whatever the orientation of the photo and the printout options, the bowing of a wide-angle lens corrected first. Tables that writing between them runs together into one blot are cut apart where the blot's ink thins out across it (side by side, or two by two), or, notes written in the margin between them filling the gap, where the tables' own long lines stop. In the live view, the sheet is followed through the video frame after frame, whatever the camera does (moved, turned, brought closer, lost from sight and found again), by keypoints of the print and the writing; its grids are drawn over the video, each in its colour with its archer once known, while the slow work (grids, headers, cells, checks) is done in a worker, never stopping the video. Each cell is read as soon as the camera shows it large and sharp enough, again when it shows it better, the readings of each cell put together; a cell read for sure takes a green veil. Each grid is put back on its own printed lines now and then (the header row and the number column bound the table), so that its outline keeps the table's shape as the camera moves. As soon as the sheet's cards are identified, they open by themselves with their arrows, from a frame showing them whole, and keep being brought up to date as the camera goes on. The next sheet can be shown without stopping the camera: when the sheet is lost for more than a moment, or when the header of a card identified, read again now and then (at once when its cells read otherwise than they did), shows another archer, or when the grids are found again elsewhere than the cards (a camera that stays where it is, the sheet changed under it), or when the sheet leaves the camera's field (no grid found any more where the cards lie whole, the camera still, the table's lines lost), the view starts afresh on the new one; so it does when two grids lie over each other (impossible on a sheet: the following or a fit has gone wrong), and a card newly identified on another target than the others has their headers read again at once. A card with no archer's name printed is not tried every second for ever, and a header to read again comes before those of the cards not known yet. A header is read as soon as its name and club lines are in the frame, its target's box cut by the frame's edge or not (a header not found there then tells nothing of another sheet), and a header seen leaning a degree or two is straightened before it is read. The live view works on frames of 1920 pixels at most (a phone's 4K made it four times slower, nothing better read); a photo taken with the button keeps the camera's full size. While the camera moves, the page says to hold it still: cells are read on still frames. A legend under the video tells what is drawn over it; each card's label lies on its header's side, by the name, however the sheet lies (a sheet turned over no longer has it over its total row); a cell drawn red tells a sure mistake: an arrow read for sure that ianseo holds otherwise (an entry mistake), or a running total or total that the arrows, all sure up to it, do not make (an addition mistake on the sheet). Three modes with the camera, in one window that also shows an imported picture. Automatic: the camera fixed, facing the table (only the sheets move); until the grids are found, the view is greyed but where to lay them; once every grid of the sheet is seen whole and readable (header, cells, totals) and the view is still, the picture takes itself (a white flash), the cards identified by the live view first if they can be within a few seconds; the window freezes on it, read as a photo, and folds away for the cards to take the page, until "Back to the live view" for the next sheet. Manual: the same, the picture taken on "Take the picture". Video: read as the video goes, the camera in hand. In the automatic mode, the sheet is not followed: the view of the moment is compared with the one before, so that a sheet changed, moved or taken away is seen as soon as it is let go, and nothing is read while a sheet is handled (once grids are found, only their area compared, brightness and contrast evened out: a thing passing beside the sheets, or the camera's exposure setting itself, disturbs nothing); each cell is read once, in large batches, as from a photo (those still in doubt a few times more), and an arrow is sure from the first check of a card read whole. Nothing to set before the first sheet: the places of a sheet's grids read whole are kept by themselves (shown before the next ones are found), for the competition and the camera, and the first whole sheet's tables give their size (a grid of another size left out: part of a table, two tables run together). The lens of a camera whose bowing the lines' measure misses is searched for by the grids it lets fit the competition's layouts (not only found), from 0.1 to 0.6. The picture shown can be turned over or mirrored (display only), and the window folded away (nothing drawn then, the reading going on). Each cell reframed on its own lines before it is read in the video mode only (each border set on the nearest line found in a margin around the cell: more sure cells from the video, nothing gained on a picture). Options for the module's development: showing what is being looked at in the video mode (cells read, cells in doubt, cells and header being read; always shown in the other modes; on at first), recording the trial (the video and what the page made of it, in the server's temporary directory for 7 days), and sending the cells in doubt (on at first) to the new page Cells to check, where a person types what is written, a few dozen cells at a time, each shown large with its neighbours, its target and distance, what it is on the card and the highest number it can hold (a number its archer's face cannot make flagged), for the reading networks to learn from (60 days); a cell cut out badly is told by a click or by "*", on the number pad; the total row is named as what the archer signs, with the card's own labels. Only grids that match one of the competition's layouts are kept, the fit most detections agree with. ISK's QR code, when printed on the sheet, gives its target, session and distance (read by the browser, or by jsQR, Apache License 2.0, shipped in assets/js/vendor/); the archer is identified by the scorecard's barcode, or else by the target and the name printed on it (the target read first, the name checking it among the archers of that target; an archer of another session than the one chosen is pointed out, with a button to switch), or by the target typed in (in the live view, once a card of the sheet is identified, the others are read among the archers left on that target, and a card beside it is given the archer its place on the sheet calls for, unless its name reads otherwise, four cards side by side or two by two; the ends shot are told by six arrows, the first two of an end empty and of the next and the card's last two (read empty 0.85 sure: an empty card is no longer read whole), and those not shot are not read; a cell in doubt is read again three times at most until the camera shows it better; a cell read for sure on two checks in a row keeps its value and is not read again, unless the card as a whole falls in doubt); every cell is cut out of the photo and shown beside what ianseo holds.

A camera whose bowing the straightness of the grid lines does not reveal (the grids then found one or two of three, or none) has its lens searched for by the grids it shows: the view still a moment with fewer grids than the sheet holds, the frame is straightened by a few lenses side by side in the reading workers and the one showing the most grids kept, remembered for that camera. The automatic picture waits for the cards to come back from the server once the archers are identified (a moment), so as to be read from the live view's fits; a grid the live view had fitted and identified that the picture's own analysis misses is read from the live view's fit, not left out. The archers per sheet (renamed so) offer only what the core prints for the competition's sessions (two side by side up to two archers per target, three for three, five or six, four otherwise) and follow the session chosen; no target is typed any more (a card whose header cannot be read is offered the archers left on the sheet's target); the automatic imports are named "by archer" and "by sheet". A card's head holds its actions, category, club and what ianseo holds, right of the archer and the totals; the writing into ianseo is offered once the quick checks are done, and the buttons come again on the Total row; an end's sum, running total or count read unsurely is framed yellow, apart from the arrows and the signed totals (orange). Speed: a picture's cells are read by workers side by side (assets/js/pool.js, read-worker.js: the computer's cores but one or two, at most 8; the page left free; the same readings), every card of a sheet at once; the automatic picture of a fixed camera, every grid fitted and identified by the live view, is read from those fits with no second analysis (the rows one line over, each way, kept for a reading in doubt), each card fetched again from ianseo first; the grid's lines refined on the points near each line only (a sheet of three cards read in about 0.9 s instead of 3 to 6 s once the picture is taken, on a recent computer). A picture's grids are looked for by several workers at once (each works the picture out, then takes its share of the blots that may be tables, put together in their order: the same grids), in the live view too (its worker has helpers of its own), and once the sheet's grids are all found the analysis stops there; the analysis itself and the reading of the numbers made cheaper, with the same results; the headers of a picture's cards read side by side, the cards fitted in the sheet's order and read together, the sheet's ISK code read by a worker meanwhile (on a computer of eight threads, the live view's search for the grids went from about 13.6 s to 3 s, a sheet read from a picture from about 20 s to 6 to 8 s). The trial's log tells the computer's threads and the time of each step of a reading. The picture is read from the live view's fits once every grid is fitted, though a card is not identified yet (it waits for the operator, the archers left on the target offered); a picture's headers are read the sheet's one way first, whose card each tells and each barcode found by the workers beside them; the workers analyse before their networks are loaded, each analysis's work going to the workers that have worked its picture out, its second pass started early when it is sure to be wanted (the same grids); the cells the live view read for sure are not read again. A card not identified takes the letter of its place in the sheet's own reading order (A > B > C whichever way the sheet lies; two rows of two for four). More grids found on a picture than the sheet holds (a keyboard's keys beside it): those that fit the competition's layouts best are kept. The camera is asked for 1920 x 1080 (what the reading uses), and a tablet, a phone or a computer of little memory starts fewer workers; workers that do not answer within 20 s are left, the analysis done on its own. The lens is searched for only once the view has looked for its grids, the lens of now tried first. The live view's worker is started afresh when it is not up within 15 s, and the reading workers start after it. The networks' convolutions run in WebAssembly SIMD where the browser has it (a small module written out with the module, three to five times faster; the same readings), a cell read in about half the time; the live view's headers are read side by side by its worker's helpers. The live view's worker started afresh for real (its lens sent plain: a restart used to stop the view). The capture bar: the modes, a triangle that folds the view, pictos to take the picture, go back to the live view and stop the camera; the view turned by quarters and mirrored from its corners; on a phone or a tablet, the page at the screen's width, larger buttons, and only the phone's own camera offered (Photo) beside the triangle. Read again, among each card's actions: its grid read a line lower, then a line higher, then looked for again on the photo cut around the card, closer (at once when no grid was fitted or no archer told), the card then read again; a place without a grid, or a photo without any, has the whole photo searched again. The cells' pictures are underlined (thick orange in doubt, thin yellow for the checks only) and their height set with a bar; a running total, a sum or a count of tens and Xs of an end wrong or not what ianseo holds is framed orange, red kept for the arrows and the Total row's signed totals; the ends' column has no heading and Total is written upwards; a signed total left blank where the arrows make 0 has a single = 0 button; correcting an arrow offers the face's values highest first (X, 10, 9... M), blank last; the card's head without its line of category, club and what ianseo holds. The development tools (series capture, cells to check, the reading page's trial options) are hidden until the administrator chooses Become a developer on the module's update page (a row of the core's Parameters, OcrDevTools); hidden, their pages and endpoints refuse to serve. The networks' sums (assets/js/nn.js, shared by the readers of the cells and of the printed text) go four output channels at a time, the same sums in the same order: the arrow network 2.4 times faster, the text ones 1.5 to 1.8 times, a sheet of three cards read a quarter faster. The handwritten values are read in the browser by three small neural networks shipped with the module (arrows; single digits; numbers read whole, which need no parting of digits that touch or run into each other), trained on the EMNIST handwriting of NIST, then on photos of real scorecards labelled by their competition's arrows and on the cells checked on the page Cells to check (an X written "+" or "10+" is read as an X). Each cell is cut out with a margin: a stroke running over from it is read with it, one from the next cell left out, the grid's lines taken out. Touching digits are parted along the lightest way between them, and numbers are also read whole, the two readings combined. Each written number is read among the values its cell can hold with the archer's own target face at that distance (three arrows make 30 at most, and on a face scoring 6 to 10 neither 1 to 5 nor 11; a running total only what the arrows shot so far can make; a count no more than the arrows it counts). The readings are then checked: the sums, running totals and counts the archer wrote decide between doubtful readings, the arrows being what counts; a count of 10s or Xs left blank weighs little, as archers often forget it, and a line's sum cell holding the whole end's total (written there instead, on an end shot over two lines) is read as such, its own cell then left blank making the card no less sure, and shown right. A running total written across the end's total cell and its own (its hundreds in the first, "1 | 12" for 112, or "24 | 9" over the line between), one person writing a whole sheet so, is read as one number when the sheet's numbers then agree better (such a sheet showed every cell in doubt). A grid set a line off shows by the cells the core prints grey (the header row over the arrows, the end numbers' column, not the distance cell above it): its lines are moved at once, the right way (on a webcam's photos, cards read all right 210 to 224 of 246, arrows right 97.8 to 99.4 %, none of the grids read soundly moved); on ends of two lines, the cells the core crosses out confirm it (their crosses on the lines that close an end): a reading still in doubt is read again one line over (the other way too when the first is no better, the table's lines telling up from down only barely; a card the live view knew read from the photo alone then), and kept if sound. All grids of a sheet face one way (header up, Total row down): one found the other way up from the others is fitted again their way, or left out. The grey cells are drawn purple where the grid is taken to lie. Arrows written out of order in most ends of two lines (archers write them highest first, nearly always) tell a grid set a line off, as do the ends' totals mostly read blank. The total row is what the archer signs (the points and the counts of the whole card): left blank, it stays blank and shows yellow to tell the operator so (over the video too); wrong, the right total is kept and shows red, the paper sheet to be corrected; read otherwise than the arrows give (or ianseo holds), not wrong for sure, it is framed orange, to check, never taken silently; it is sent to be checked only when read unsurely. Sure values show in green, values to check in orange, arrows that differ from ianseo are framed in red, and an addition mistake of the archer, carried on to the later running totals and the Total row, is flagged on those totals. A reading whose written numbers agree too little with the arrows (a blurred or too small photo), or whose ends' totals mostly read blank (a grid set a line off), is shown as uncertain throughout, never as sure; nor are the arrows of an end where the checks have the archer add wrong. A click on an arrow offers the values of the archer's target face to correct it. Saving into ianseo comes next.

Photos from a poor camera (an old webcam: soft, noisy, washed out) are handled too: when the pale printed lines of the grid escape the first threshold, a second one finds them. With a webcam, the scorecard laid sideways fills the picture and reads as well as a phone photo.

Series capture: the camera stays on and every scorecard shown is photographed as soon as its grid is found and stays still, with a beep, the next one following without any action. The photos are kept in the server's temporary directory for the open competition, deleted after 7 days, and can be downloaded as one ZIP archive. Without the live camera, the phone's own camera takes them one at a time, and photos already taken are sent many at once.

The live camera needs a secure page, and a local ianseo is used over plain http: the pages explain the Chrome setting, made once on each device, that allows it without changing the server.

The sheet's cards are shown side by side in letter order (a place without archer marked), each with a button coloured as it stands (green: all sure, right, as ianseo holds; orange: cells to check; red: a sure mistake; moving blue: being read), the reading's eye, the three totals each with its sign (checked, cross: the archer's addition mistake, warning: not what ianseo holds; green or red when sure, orange when not) and the number of alerts; a legend tells it all. Each cell's picture is framed orange when in doubt, crossed when not read; each written number shows read / calculated, and what ianseo holds in blue; each signed total can be set by the operator to what the arrows make ("= value", a total misread or the archer's mistake kept right), or to 0 when left blank (blank counts 0, no recount), and undone. Correcting an arrow offers the face's values or "blank". Two quick checks per card: the arrows in doubt taken as read in one click (those other than in ianseo left out), then, every arrow sure, the three totals set to what the arrows make. Two cards of a photo are never given one archer (a card the live view knew matched by its place in the frame's own pixels; one archer for two cards stops the writing).

Writing into ianseo, on the operator's click or automatically as ticked (the whole sheet once all sure, or each archer once sure): "Import the data" while ianseo does not hold every arrow of the distance (none, or some missing: the first whole reading; the arrows held must be the reading's but those the operator corrected; arrows and totals, the totals calculated again from the arrows, a blank signed total set to 0 counting 0), "Validate the data" once it does, by a later reading (confirmed as the core's barcode check does, only when the reading is what is entered, the cells the operator corrected written first); a value read otherwise than ianseo holds is never written nor validated, and ianseo's totals of a partial entry are shown, not compared. A grid printed at a place without archer holds back neither the whole sheet's import nor the return to live; a write refused is not tried again by itself (the card shows what ianseo holds then). Every write goes through the open competition's entries, the ranks calculated again by the core's classes as after an ISK import. The sheet written in full, the view goes back to live; the sheet left under the camera is not taken again until the view changes.

On the reading page the photo is analysed in the browser and never sent to the server. The module creates no table; it writes only into the qualification scores, as said above.
